Testimony of Brynne O'Neal Regulatory Policy Specialist, Maine State Nurses Association / National Nurses United
IN SUPPORT OF LD 2049, An Act to Clarify Indemnification When Seeking Remedy for Labor Law Violations
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Labor Hearing: Jan 27, 2026, at 1:00 p.m.
Dear Chair Tipping, Chair Roeder, and distinguished members of the Committee on Labor,
On behalf of more than 4,000 registered nurses and health care professionals providing direct patient care in our state, the Maine State Nurses Association/National Nurses United (MSNA) urges the Committee to support LD 2049.
Nurse staffing agencies employ registered nurses to work in hospitals and other settings. While colloquially these employees are often referred to as temporary staff, in practice they may work in one setting for months at a time. When one employer controls the work environment and tasks while a staffing agency is the employer of record and responsible for wages and conditions, sometimes it can be difficult for workers to vindicate their rights.
The employer where the worker goes to work every day has functional control over whether they get their breaks, the occupational health and safety of the workplace, and many other key labor rights. They should bear the same responsibility as the staffing agency for those rights. If the employer ends up paying penalties, it will then be able to be refunded by the agency under the indemnification provision, unless the two decide otherwise while contracting. In nursing, construction, and all industries, employers should be responsible for respecting the labor rights of the people who get the work done, regardless of subcontracting arrangements.
Therefore, we ask for your support on LD 2049.
Sincerely,
Brynne O'Neal Regulatory Policy Specialist, Maine State Nurses Association / National Nurses United

We support LD 2049, HP 1327 (hereinafter "LD 2049"). I will focus my comments on the need for upper-tier contractor joint and several liability for wage theft.
Growing lawlessness in the construction industry
There is growing lawlessness in the United States involving construction employers failing to pay wages, state and federal employment taxes, unemployment insurance and workers' compensation premiums. Malign construction employers have developed a lucrative and successful model to evade their obligations under the law that relies on layers of subcontractors and labor providers (who we call "labor brokers"). In the model, subcontractors use labor brokers that break the law, thus providing lower labor costs and a shield against liability. Oftentimes, labor brokers run out of money to pay employees because subcontractors pad their pockets further by not paying the brokers.1

Construction Industry Wage Theft Responsibility
The proposal before the Committee is based on similar legislation enacted in ten states and the District of Columbia.18 The legislation seeks to cut through the layers and defensive shields used to evade responsibility by making contractors and the contractor's subcontractor jointly and severally liable for violations of Chapter 15 and 7. Testimony of the Maine Real Estate and Development Association In Opposition to LD 2049, As Amended
February 10, 2026
Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, and Honorable members of the Labor Committee:
My name is Elizabeth Frazier, and I am testifying on behalf of the Maine Real Estate and Development Association (MEREDA) in opposition to LD 2049, as amended. While MEREDA supports fair and timely payment for workers, the amendment to this bill dramatically expands liability in a way that exposes homeowners and property owners to severe risk and will materially increase the cost of creating housing in Maine.
The amendment rolls developers, property owners, and even homeowners into a wage-andhour enforcement framework that was never designed to apply outside a direct employment relationship. In doing so, it creates consequences that are disproportionate, unworkable, and ultimately harmful to Maine residents.
� First and foremost, the amendment places ordinary homeowners at significant and unreasonable risk. Under a wage-and-hour enforcement model, remedies can include bank account freezes, garnishment, and other aggressive collection tools. As amended, this bill would allow those remedies to be directed at owners -- including homeowners -- who have fully paid their general contractor but have no knowledge of or control over payment disputes further down the contracting chain. This effectively turns homeowners into guarantors of wage compliance for individuals they never hired and cannot supervise.
� Second, this framework penalizes people who act responsibly and in good faith. A homeowner who pays a contractor to repair a roof, fix a plumbing issue, or renovate a kitchen could still face serious financial consequences if a subcontractor or lower-tier worker is not paid. That outcome is not only inequitable, it undermines basic notions of fairness and consumer protection -- particularly for seniors, first-time homeowners, and lower-income households.
� Third, the amendment will significantly increase the cost and difficulty of creating housing in Maine. By expanding wage-and-hour liability to owners and developers, the bill makes construction and redevelopment projects far harder to insure. Insurance markets take time to adapt to new liability regimes, and during that period coverage is often unavailable or prohibitively expensive. Those costs do not disappear -- they are passed

directly into project budgets, rents, and home prices. At a time when Maine is struggling with a severe housing shortage, this bill moves in exactly the wrong direction. � Fourth, the amendment duplicates existing remedies while creating new problems. Subcontractors already have access to strong protections under Maine's mechanic's lien laws, which allow for super-priority liens against real property when payment disputes arise. That system is specifically designed to balance the interests of workers, owners, lenders, and consumers. LD 2049, as amended, overlays a far more punitive enforcement regime without demonstrating that existing tools are insufficient. � Fifth, the amendment creates uncertainty in the housing and real estate market. If owners can be subject to wage-and-hour liability for work performed on their property, real estate transactions become more complicated and riskier. Absent some form of certification that every worker down the contracting chain has been paid, buyers, lenders, and insurers will hesitate. That uncertainty slows transactions, increases costs, and reduces housing mobility statewide.
Finally, while the amendment may be motivated by a legitimate concern involving a bad actor, it responds by imposing broad, disproportionate liability on homeowners and property owners across Maine. The result is a policy that discourages renovation, redevelopment, and new construction -- all of which are essential to addressing Maine's housing shortage.
For these reasons, MEREDA respectfully urges the Committee to oppose LD 2049 as amended.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Elizabeth M. Frazier
On behalf of the Maine Real Estate and Development Association

Testimony in Support of LD 2049, "An Act to Clarify Indemnification When Seeking Remedy for Labor Law Violations" James Myall, Policy Analyst February 10, 2026
Good afternoon, Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Labor. My name is James Myall, and I'm a policy analyst at the Maine Center for Economic Policy. I'm here to testify in support of LD 2049, "An Act to Clarify Indemnification When Seeking Remedy for Labor Law Violations," because MECEP believes that when Maine workers are mistreated, their employers shouldn't be allowed to pass the buck.
LD 2049 would ensure that when construction workers' rights on the job are violated, they can seek redress either from the subcontractor who hired them directly, or the general contractor overseeing the job as a whole. This is an important change to make sure that someone is always responsible for ensuring that workers
are paid and that their rights are protected.
The legislature has established labor laws to ensure that all workers are compensated fairly for their work and are treated with dignity. When unscrupulous employers violate these rules to give themselves an unfair advantage, it hurts both the workers and the businesses who are doing the right thing. Unfortunately, the construction industry has more instances of labor rights violations than many other industries, in part because of the prevalence of subcontracting, which brings extra pressure to down costs and makes oversight more difficult. Of the wage and hour violations recorded by the Maine Department of Labor between 2022 and 2024, construction workers accounted for 9% of those owed back wages,1 despite making up only 6% of all employees statewide.2
The fragmented nature of the construction industry with a multitude of subcontractors can also make it harder for the Department of Labor to recover lost wages or assess penalties against bad actors. When workers don't get these lost wages back, or see a significant delay in recovering what they are owed, it not only hurts them but their local communities as well. Construction projects can bring important economic benefits, particularly to rural areas, but only if workers are paid fairly and on time. LD 2049 will help to make sure those promises of economic development are fulfilled.
Thank you for your time. I urge you to vote "ought to pass" on LD 2049. I'll be happy to answer any questions.

To the Joint Standing Committee on Labor Public Hearing, 2/10/2026

Good afternoon to you, Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Labor. I am Kate Burkhart, Director of the Bureau of Labor Standards at the Maine Department of Labor. Thank you for the opportunity to provide testimony on LD 2049.

At the outset, the Department would like to acknowledge and thank the bill's sponsor for proactively reaching out to ask whether the Department had questions or suggested changes to the original bill language. At the sponsor's request, the Department subsequently provided technical drafting feedback intended to clarify statutory operation and improve administrative coherence, while preserving the sponsor's policy intent. The sponsor incorporated several of those technical suggestions. We also understand that the sponsor engaged in additional conversations with other stakeholders, and that the language before the Committee reflects amendments beyond the Department's initial technical input. While the Department is neither for nor against the language before you, we understand that a sister agency has submitted written comment that outlines some concerns with the amendment language.

As amended, LD 2049 establishes joint and several liability in two distinct contexts under Title 26. First, in the construction industry, the bill provides that contractors, owners or developers, and construction subcontractors responsible for performing or directing craft work may be jointly and severally liable for unpaid wages, liquidated damages, and interest arising from certain wage-related violations. The bill also establishes indemnification obligations between parties.

Second, the bill addresses temporary staffing and labor supply arrangements by establishing joint and several liability between employment agencies or labor brokers and the employers for whom work is performed, with respect to wage- and benefit-related violations. The amendment includes a definition of "labor broker" that focuses on the activities performed--such as recruiting, supplying, placing, or managing workers--rather than on an entity's chosen label.

As written, the bill could affect a range of Maine employers operating in construction and labor supply contexts by altering how responsibility for wage compliance may be allocated among parties in multi-entity working arrangements. The Department does not take a position on the policy merits of these changes, but notes that the framework is intended to clarify responsibility and remedies in situations involving layered employment relationships. The Department wishes to clarify for the record that LD 2049, as amended, does not create a new enforcement mandate, duty, or investigatory obligation for the Department of Labor. The bill operates through statutory liability and indemnification provisions and does not require additional staffing or enforcement activity by the Department.
We would also like to flag one technical issue that may warrant the Committee's attention, and we have notified the sponsor of our concern. Although the amendment is intended to apply broadly, the bill text places the joint and several liability provision in �1318, which is located within Maine's prevailing wage statutes. Placement in �1318 could have the effect of limiting application of the provision to prevailing wage projects only. We believe the sponsor intended for this language to apply to all covered projects.
If the Committee's intent is for the joint and several liability framework to apply to all covered projects, and not solely prevailing wage work, the Department suggests relocating the provision to a new section, �591-B, adjacent to Maine's existing employee misclassification statutes. That placement may better align the provision with other enforcement tools addressing complex employment relationships and avoid unintended limitation of scope.
Thank you for the opportunity to testify. I'd be happy to answer any questions now, or at a future work session.

Testimony of the Associated Builders and Contractors of Maine In Opposition to LD 2049, An Act to Clarify Indemnification When Seeking Remedy for
Labor Law Violations
Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Labor:
My name is Keith Herrick, and I am testifying on behalf of the Associated Builders and Contractors of Maine (ABC Maine) in opposition to LD 2049, as amended. ABC Maine represents more than 180 member companies employing thousands of Maine construction workers across the state.
The Sponsor's Amendment to LD 2049 does not improve the bill--it makes it significantly worse. While the original bill was problematic, the amended version expands liability even further by imposing automatic joint and several liability on contractors, subcontractors, owners, and developers for wage and benefit violations committed by another party.
Under the amended bill, a contractor, owner, or developer may be held fully liable for wage violations committed solely by a subcontractor--even when that party had no involvement in, control over, or knowledge of the subcontractor's payroll practices, and even when all contractual payments were made properly and on time. This is a dramatic departure from longstanding principles of independent contracting and basic fairness.
The amendment attempts to soften this expansion by allowing for indemnification. However, that provision offers little real-world protection. Wage violations most often occur when a subcontractor is already financially distressed or insolvent, making indemnification meaningless. In practice, the amended bill shifts enforcement risk, legal costs, penalties, and reputational harm upstream to parties who did not commit the violation and had no ability to prevent it.
By explicitly extending joint liability to owners and developers, the amendment will have farreaching consequences beyond the construction trades themselves. Property owners, housing developers, and project financiers will now face new and unpredictable exposure for employment decisions made by third parties. This will discourage investment, complicate project financing, increase insurance and bonding costs, and ultimately drive up the cost of housing and infrastructure in Maine.
The amendment also creates perverse incentives. Rather than improving compliance, it will push contractors and owners to avoid working with small, emerging, or minority-owned subcontractors, who are perceived as higher risk under a strict liability regime. That outcome directly undermines workforce development, competition, and opportunity in the construction industry.
Importantly, this bill remains unnecessary. Maine already has strong wage enforcement mechanisms through the Department of Labor, along with civil and criminal penalties that appropriately target employers who actually commit violations. The amended LD 2049 does not

strengthen enforcement--it merely redirects liability to parties that are easier to pursue, regardless of fault.
ABC Maine strongly supports fair pay and lawful employment practices. However, those goals can be achieved without converting contractors, owners, and developers into guarantors of third-party compliance. If the Committee believes changes are warranted, we urge a far more targeted approach--one that focuses liability on employers who knowingly participate in or direct violations, rather than imposing blanket, automatic joint liability.
For these reasons, ABC Maine respectfully urges the Committee to oppose LD 2049 as amended.
Thank you for the opportunity to testify. We would welcome the chance to work with the Committee on a more balanced and workable alternative.
Respectfully submitted,
Keith Herrick On behalf of the Associated Builders and Contractors of Maine

Dear Sen. Tipping and Rep. Roeder:
On behalf of the temporary staffing industry, we respectfully submit this letter in opposition to the proposed enactment of 26 MRSA �1318, specifically subsection 2 relating to employment agencies and employers.
The temporary staffing industry plays a critical role in Maine's economy, employing over 45,000 workers statewide, thus contributing significantly to the state's economic vitality and growth. Temporary staffing agencies connect workers with employment opportunities at no cost to the workers, providing flexibility for businesses, and helping employers respond to seasonal demand, skill shortages, and unexpected workforce needs. The proposed joint and several liability framework would significantly disrupt this model and produce unintended consequences for workers, employers, and the broader labor market.
Unfair Allocation of Liability and Risk
Under proposed Section 2, staffing agencies and client employers would be jointly and severally liable for violations of Chapter 7 and 15 of the Maine statutes, regardless of which party exercised control over the conduct giving rise to the violation. This blanket imposition of liability fails to account for the practical realities of temporary staffing arrangements, where the legal responsibilities of staffing agencies and their clients are contractually shared or allocated based on their respective relationship with and control over the worker and the work performed.
Imposing automatic joint and several liability on staffing agencies for the sweeping range of employment and construction contract obligations set forth in Chapters 7 and 15 would effectively hold agencies responsible for the myriad actions and decisions made solely by client employers--such as timekeeping practices, worksite supervision, scheduling, and compliance with workplace-specific requirements--over which the staffing agency may have limited or no control.
Chilling Effect on Workforce Access and Job Opportunities
The increased legal exposure created by this proposal will discourage staffing agencies from serving certain employers or industries, particularly small businesses and emerging enterprises that rely most heavily on

temporary staffing. As risk increases, staffing agencies may be forced to limit placements, increase costs, or withdraw from the Maine market altogether. These outcomes would directly reduce employment opportunities for Maine workers, including individuals seeking entry-level positions, flexible schedules, or pathways back into the workforce.
Duplication of Existing Enforcement Mechanisms
Maine already has robust wage and hour laws, enforcement tools, and penalties designed to protect workers and hold bad actors accountable. Expanding joint and several liability is not necessary to ensure compliance and instead creates duplicative enforcement that punishes compliant employers and staffing agencies while failing to target intentional violators more effectively. Good-faith actors should not be subjected to heightened liability for violations they did not cause and could not reasonably prevent.
Statutory Requirement for Indemnification by Employment Agency
The bill's requirement that staffing agencies indemnify their clients, "except as otherwise provided in their contract," places the agency at a distinct disadvantage when negotiating agreement terms. Indemnification provisions are critical elements in contract negotiation. Clients will have no incentive to negotiate this critical term because the statutory mandate unfairly places it in the best position possible. The client is not motivated to agree to indemnify the staffing agency for the client's violation of chapter 7 or 15 or to negotiate the indemnification terms fairly.
Recommendation
We respectfully urge the legislature to reject subsection 2 of the proposed legislation as proposed. Instead, it should be amended to recognize and preserve the distinct roles and responsibilities of staffing agencies and client employers and their historical practice of contractually allocating legal responsibility based on their respective relationship with and control over the worker. Specifically, we propose that Section 2 be amended as follows:
2. Employment agencies and employers. An employment agency that employs an employee who performs work on behalf of or for the benefit of another employer pursuant to a temporary staffing arrangement or contract for services is, together with the employer, jointly and severally liable for violation of this chapter or chapter 7 as they may mutually agree pursuant to an executed and enforceable contract between the employment agency and the employer, and the employment agency and employer. Except as otherwise provided in an executed and enforceable contract between an employment agency and an employer, the employment agency shall indemnify each other the employer for any wages, damages, interest, penalties and attorney's fees owed as a result of the employment agency's indemnitor's violation of this chapter or chapter 7 as provided in such contract.

The temporary staffing industry is committed to fair pay, lawful employment practices, and strong worker protections. We stand ready to work collaboratively with lawmakers to address any compliance concerns without undermining a vital employment model that benefits Maine's workers and businesses alike.
Thank you for your consideration.
Very truly yours,

In Opposition to LD 2049

Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, members of the Joint Standing Committee on Labor, my name is Meghan Russo, Director of Government Affairs at the Maine Department of Transportation. MaineDOT submits the following testimony in opposition to LD 2049 as amended due to concerns regarding expanded liability, legal uncertainty, and unintended consequences for public owners.
As amended, the bill establishes joint and several liability among contractors, owners or developers, and construction subcontractors for unpaid wages, liquidated damages, and interest arising from a subcontractor's violation of wage and benefit laws under Title 26, chapters 7 and 15. While the original version of the bill applied only to contractors and subcontractors, the amended version includes owners and developers, which could encompass MaineDOT as a public owner on construction projects.
The department is particularly concerned with the provision imposing liability where an owner is deemed responsible for "performing or directing craft work." The sponsor's amendment does not define what it means to "direct craft work," creating substantial ambiguity. On MaineDOT projects, the department establishes contract requirements, specifications, and performance standards, and typically has staff or consultants present on site to monitor compliance and progress. It is unclear whether these standard owner functions could be construed as "directing" craft work under the bill. This lack of clarity creates uncertainty and significantly increases the risk of litigation over threshold questions of liability, even where the department has no role in hiring, paying, or supervising subcontractor employees.
The bill's joint and several liability framework further compounds these concerns. Joint and several liability permits recovery of the full amount of unpaid wages and associated damages from any one of the liable parties, regardless of fault. In practice, this means that MaineDOT

could be required to pay wages owed by a subcontractor over which it has no employment relationship and no control over payroll practices.
MaineDOT fully supports the goal of ensuring that workers are paid lawfully and on time. However, the amended bill shifts responsibility away from the parties that control payroll and employment practices and onto owners, including public entities, that lack the practical ability to prevent or remedy wage violations by subcontractors. This approach risks increasing project costs, discouraging bidders, and diverting public funds from transportation infrastructure to cover private wage disputes.
For these reasons, MaineDOT respectfully urges the Committee to oppose the bill as amended or to reconsider the inclusion of owners and developers, particularly public owners, within the scope of joint and several liability.
Thank you for the opportunity to submit testimony. MaineDOT would be happy to be available at the work session to answer any questions regarding our testimony and/or opposition.

Re: Testimony in Opposition to LD 2049 An Act to Clarify Indemnification When Seeking Remedy for Labor Law Violations
Dear Senator Tipping, Representative Roeder, and Members of the Committee on Labor:
The Maine Water Utilities Association (MWUA) appreciates the opportunity to provide testimony in opposition to LD 2049 as amended by the sponsor's amendment dated February 9, 2026. According to the sponsor's amendment, an owner of a construction project will be jointly and severally liable, along with a contractor and subcontractor, to a subcontractor's employees for any unpaid wages or compensation, including indemnification for damages or compensation owed due to the subcontractor's violation of certain labor laws, unless the violation was due to lack of prompt payment by the owner or contractor to the subcontractor.
Given that water utilities in Maine are frequently the "owner" of numerous multi-million dollar construction projects in the State that are needed to ensure safe, potable drinking water for Maine consumers, we are very concerned that this amendment would make water utilities liable for the activities of subcontractors over which utilities have no control, and further, that the cost of such liability would ultimately flow through to water utility customers in their regular water bills.
About MWUA. MWUA is a nonprofit association based in Augusta that provides support for water works professionals throughout the State of Maine in advocating for safe drinking water through educational and technical programming as well as advocacy on the local, state, and national level. The Association was formed in 1925 and consists of approximately 86 utility and 60 associate members. Maine's water utilities provide service to approximately 700,000 Maine residents, thousands of Maine businesses and public institutions, and millions of visitors to Maine every year.
Discussion. Section 1 of the proposed law is broad and would make an owner of a project, such as a water utility, responsible for payment to employees of a subcontractor of wages, penalties and interest if that subcontractor violated provisions of chapter 15, including the subcontractor's failure to pay wages owed. We certainly understand that the subcontractor itself has and should have liability for such violations. However, project owners do not have direct contractual relationships with subcontractors who are employed by contractors. Rather, the relationship

Testimony of MWUA against LD 2049 February 17, 2026 Page 2
between owner and subcontractor is two steps removed, meaning that the project owner has no direct control over a subcontractor's actions; the direct contractual relationship is between the contractor and the subcontractor. In this relationship, the owner does not interfere with the contractor-subcontractor relationship and rightfully expects that relationship to be controlled by the contractor.
This bill would fundamentally change the project owner-subcontractor relationship by introducing the risk of liability to the owner for a subcontractor's failure to compensate their employees for a variety of circumstances. To manage this risk, project owners would need to exercise direct control over subcontractors, and project owners would need to build into contracts the risk of subcontractor malfeasance.
Applied to the context of water utilities, the great majority of whom are quasi-municipal entities, water utilities would need to increase the cost of their construction projects, perhaps through insurance, to take into the account the risk that subcontractors fail to properly compensate their employees. And for those utilities who cannot or do not factor in these risks, the utility could later become directly liable for any unpaid compensation to subcontractor employees.
Finally, it is important to understand that most water utilities are not private employers. Most are quasi-municipal entities that are units of government. So, if a consumer-owned water utility becomes liable for subcontractor employee compensation, the liability ultimately becomes the responsibility of water utility customers who must pay for the liability through higher water rates - because there is no other entity able to absorb or pay for these costs. And even for those water utilities who are privately owned, their liabilities represent the cost of operating the utility, and such costs would ultimately be passed through to customers in rates.
Overall, we believe it is inequitable and unjust to have the ratepayers of a water utility be financially responsible for the actions of subcontractor with regard to their employees when the utility has no direct relationship with the subcontractor and does not have leverage over its actions.
Conclusion. This bill is overbroad and has potential unintended consequences to ratepayers. We respectfully urge the committee to vote LD 2049 ought not to pass.
Thank you for your consideration,
Michael Cummons, Chair MWUA Legislative & Regulatory Affairs Committee
